blocks.text: Duplicate rows sneak into real datasets more often than you would expect. A pipeline retries after a timeout and writes the same batch twice. Two data sources get merged and they overlap. A logging system double records an event. A user double clicks submit on a form. Whatever the cause, you end up with rows that should not be there, and pandas gives you a clean, small toolkit for finding and removing them.

blocks.alt: A data pipeline running twice and writing the same rows into a dataset twice
blocks.caption: This is the single most common real world cause of duplicate rows.

items: A data pipeline runs twice, either from a retry after a failure or a scheduling mistake.
Two overlapping data sources get merged, and some rows exist in both.
A logging system retries a failed write and ends up recording the same event twice.
A form gets submitted twice by an accidental double click.

blocks.text: .duplicated() returns a boolean Series flagging which rows are duplicates. It does not flag every copy by default, it flags only the EXTRA copies, controlled by the keep parameter.

blocks.alt: duplicated with keep set to first flagging the second occurrence while keeping the first as not flagged
blocks.caption: The default: the first copy is treated as the real one, later copies are flagged.

blocks.alt: duplicated with keep set to last flagging the first occurrence instead and keeping the last
blocks.caption: Flip it around: treat the last copy as the real one.

blocks.alt: duplicated with keep set to False flagging every occurrence of a duplicated row including the first
blocks.caption: Useful when you want to inspect every copy of a duplicate, not just the extras.

blocks.content: {"headers":["keep value","Behavior"],"rows":[["first (default)","Marks the second and later occurrences as duplicates, keeps the first"],["last","Marks the first and earlier occurrences as duplicates, keeps the last"],["False","Marks every occurrence of a duplicated row, including the first"]]}

blocks.text: .drop_duplicates() removes the rows that .duplicated() would have flagged, and it accepts the exact same keep parameter.

blocks.alt: drop_duplicates removing the rows that were flagged as duplicates
blocks.caption: The natural next step after duplicated: actually get rid of the extras.

blocks.text: 4. Matching on a Subset of Columns

By default, both duplicated() and drop_duplicates() require every single column to match before they call two rows duplicates. In practice, that is often too strict. subset lets you check only the columns that actually determine whether two rows represent the same real world thing.

blocks.alt: Matching on only a subset of columns catching duplicates that a full row match would have missed
blocks.caption: A shared ID or email is often what actually makes two rows the same event, not every column.

blocks.alt: Two rows sharing the same event id but with slightly different timestamps still representing one underlying event
blocks.caption: A full row match would miss this, since the timestamps differ, but the subset match catches it correctly.

blocks.title: subset is what you use most in practice
blocks.content: Exact full row matching is rare in real data. Almost every real deduplication task comes down to picking the right subset of columns that actually identifies a unique record.

blocks.text: Exact matching, even with a subset, only catches rows that are byte for byte identical in the columns you checked. Real data is messier than that. 'Acme Corp' and 'acme corp ' with trailing whitespace represent the same company but will not match exactly.

blocks.alt: Two values representing the same real world thing failing an exact match due to capitalization and whitespace
blocks.caption: Exact matching alone will miss this pair entirely.

blocks.title: A thorough dedup strategy needs string cleaning too
blocks.content: Catching near duplicates like this usually means normalizing text first, lowercasing, stripping whitespace, before you check for duplicates. The upcoming String Operations lesson in this module covers exactly these cleaning techniques.

blocks.text: Before you drop anything, it is worth knowing how big the problem actually is. Chaining .sum() onto duplicated() gives you a fast count.

blocks.alt: duplicated summed to give a total count of how many duplicate rows exist before deciding what to do
blocks.caption: Know the scale of the problem before you act on it.

blocks.text: Say you have a signups DataFrame where the same email address shows up more than once, each with a slightly different signup_timestamp, most likely from a retried signup flow.

code.content:
signups.duplicated(subset=["email"]).sum()
# 214

deduped = signups.drop_duplicates(subset=["email"], keep="first")
# keeps whichever signup came first for each email

blocks.alt: A user signups DataFrame deduplicated down to one row per unique email using subset based matching
blocks.caption: keep=first keeps the earliest signup for each email, which is usually the one you actually want.

blocks.text: If you instead wanted the most recent signup per email, keep='last' would flip that choice, or you could sort by timestamp before deduplicating to be certain about which row survives.

items: duplicated() flags rows, drop_duplicates() removes them, both share the same keep parameter.
keep controls which occurrence survives: first, last, or none with keep=False to see every copy.
subset checks only the columns that actually determine uniqueness, which is what most real deduplication actually needs.
Exact matching still misses near duplicates from capitalization or whitespace, which needs string cleaning first.
Count duplicates with duplicated().sum() before deciding how aggressively to deduplicate.
